name: Going Concern Analysis
title: Going Concern Analysis
answer: Going concern analysis in continuous audit and assurance is the ongoing evaluation of whether an entity can meet its obligations and continue operating for the foreseeable future. It covers management's cash flow forecasts, liquidity headroom, debt covenants, contingent liabilities, and the reasonableness of assumptions about revenue, costs, and financing. In a continuous setting the analysis is not a single year end exercise, it is a monitored position with triggers, thresholds, and periodic refresh. The work sits with auditors, management, and audit committees, and it draws on financial, operational, and market evidence.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Going concern analysis in continuous audit and assurance is the ongoing evaluation of whether an entity can meet its obligations and continue operating for the foreseeable future. It covers management's cash flow forecasts, liquidity headroom, debt covenants, contingent liabilities, and the reasonableness of assumptions about revenue, costs, and financing. In a continuous setting the analysis is not a single year end exercise, it is a monitored position with triggers, thresholds, and periodic refresh. The work sits with auditors, management, and audit committees, and it draws on financial, operational, and market evidence.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a connected set of financial and operational data: general ledger and ERP extracts, bank and treasury feeds, debt and covenant schedules, rolling cash flow forecasts, accounts payable and receivable aging, and budget versus actual reports. Market data, credit spreads, news, and regulatory filings can be pulled in where they affect liquidity or financing. AI components typically include anomaly detection over transactions, natural language processing over earnings calls and filings, and scenario engines that stress test cash flow assumptions. The output is usually a dashboard or a monitored scorecard that feeds audit documentation and management reporting.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method starts with defining the assessment period and the entity's available liquidity, then obtaining management's cash flow forecast and the assumptions behind it. The team tests those assumptions against historical performance, current backlog, covenant terms, and plausible downside scenarios. Continuous monitoring adds automated alerts when cash, covenant headroom, or key ratios move outside set thresholds, which prompts a fresh review. Findings are documented with the evidence, the model version, and the judgment applied, and they are escalated when the conclusion changes. The aim is a timely, evidence based view of whether the going concern basis remains appropriate.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Governance covers data rights, confidentiality, model risk, and the provenance of every input and output. The analysis relies on management representations, audited figures, and third party data, so the audit trail must show where each number came from and who approved it. Model outputs are not conclusions on their own, they are inputs to professional judgment, and they need validation, version control, and clear ownership. Independence and confidentiality rules apply, especially when continuous monitoring touches sensitive treasury or covenant data. The risk of over reliance on a single forecast or a black box model is managed through documentation, challenge, and human review.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Going concern analysis is moving toward more frequent, data driven monitoring rather than an annual or quarterly snapshot. Expect tighter integration between audit platforms and ERP, treasury, and covenant systems, so that liquidity and covenant headroom are visible in near real time. AI will increasingly handle anomaly detection, scenario generation, and narrative extraction, while professionals focus on judgment, challenge, and communication. Regulatory and standard setters are likely to expect stronger evidence of continuous assessment and clearer disclosure of the assumptions used. The direction is toward earlier warning, better provenance, and a closer link between going concern conclusions and the entity's own risk management.
